items.q: What problem does a distributed lock solve, and what does it leave to the rest of the system?
items.a:
A distributed lock is a coordination primitive: for a named resource, it lets competing processes agree that one claimant may start a critical section. It is useful for reducing duplicate schedulers, serialising a repair, or protecting a non-transactional resource for a bounded interval. It does not make a remote side effect atomic, does not roll back work after a process dies, and does not stop an old holder that keeps running after its lease expires. That last distinction is why a lock alone is not a correctness boundary.
QuestionWhat a lock can answerWhat it cannot promise alone
CoordinationWho may enter now?That the winner will finish
FailureWhen may another claimant try?That the old claimant has stopped
Business invariantHow to reduce concurrent attemptsThat money, inventory or a remote write is correct
:::tip The rule that survives production Lock for coordination. Put correctness in the authority that owns the invariant: a database constraint, a conditional write, a version check, or a downstream system that enforces a fencing token. ::: :::deep - A lock is often a good admission control: it prevents ten replicas from starting the same expensive rebuild. - A unique constraint or conditional update is a better correctness control: it rejects the eleventh write even if the network split the lock holders. - If the protected resource cannot observe ownership, expiry and fencing, the lock service is only making a best effort. - This is the same boundary as the distributed-transaction answer: keep the strong invariant local where possible, and make the asynchronous edge idempotent (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q5). :::

items.q: How are safety, liveness and fairness different in a lock protocol?
items.a:
Treat these as separate review questions instead of calling every successful acquire safe.
PropertyMeaningTypical design evidence
SafetyTwo valid owners must not perform a protected action at the same time.unique ownership, compare-and-delete, fencing checked by the resource
LivenessA dead owner must not block everyone forever.lease expiry, session death, bounded wait, retry policy
FairnessA waiting claimant should not be starved indefinitely.queueing or ordered acquisition; not guaranteed by a basic key lock
ObservabilityThe team can tell whether the protocol is healthy.wait, hold, renewal, expiry and rejection metrics
A protocol can be live but unsafe: a short TTL frees a key quickly while a paused old process is still writing. It can be safe but unusable: a lock that never expires preserves mutual exclusion by blocking the whole system. Fairness is an additional promise; SET NX or an advisory lock does not automatically provide FIFO ordering. :::warn Do not collapse the properties into one word Ask which property the requirement needs, which failure breaks it, and which component enforces it. A client-side timeout is not proof of safety, and a successful lock acquisition is not proof that the resource accepted the work. ::: :::deep For each lock, write the failure contract before choosing a library: - Safety breach: two owners run. Is the side effect rejected, deduplicated, or merely logged? - Liveness breach: nobody runs. Who detects it, and how long until recovery? - Fairness breach: one tenant waits forever. Is that acceptable, or does work need a durable queue? - Visibility breach: the lock is contended but no one knows. Which alert fires before users notice? :::

items.q: What is the difference between a mutex, a lease and leader election?
items.a:
The words describe different ownership lifecycles, even though products often expose similar APIs.
PrimitiveOwnership endsGood fitMain trap
MutexExplicit unlock, or a server-side cleanup ruleShort local or transactional critical sectionsA crashed client can leave a permanent lock
LeaseExpiry unless renewedWork that must recover after a dead processThe old process may continue after expiry
Leader electionSession/lease loss or resignationOne active scheduler/controller with standby replicasLeadership is not permission to write arbitrary state
Use a mutex when the holder can reliably reach a release point. Use a lease when recovery from crash matters and the work is restartable. Use leader election when one replica should make decisions for a role, not when every resource key needs a single global owner. A lease is a time-bounded claim maintained by the coordinator. It is not a promise from the process that it will stop executing at the deadline. If the protected resource needs strict ordering, add a monotonically increasing fencing token and make the resource reject stale tokens. :::tip Choose by ownership shape Per-resource exclusivity points to a lock. One active controller points to election. A stream of independent work points to a durable queue or database claim. Do not turn all three into one Redis key. ::: :::deep Kubernetes uses Lease objects for node heartbeats and leader election; etcd elections attach leadership to a lease. That pattern is strong for selecting an active controller because the coordinator owns the session. It still needs idempotent controller actions and a resource-side guard when a stale controller can issue writes. :::

items.q: Why can a lease expire while its holder is still running?
items.a:
A process can stop making progress without stopping. Common causes include a long garbage-collection pause, CPU starvation, a frozen VM, a blocked event loop, a broken network path or a partition can prevent renewals. The coordinator observes a missed deadline and grants the lease to B. A then resumes with stale beliefs. 
T0  A acquires lease L, expires at T0 + 30s
T1  A pauses for 35s; its thread has not been killed
T2  coordinator expires L and grants it to B
T3  B writes the resource
T4  A resumes and writes with its old ownership belief
A TTL removed deadlock, but it did not remove stale work.
The safe response is not to make the TTL enormous. Keep the critical section bounded, renew with a margin, stop when renewal is lost, and make the resource reject stale fencing tokens. If no resource can enforce that token, the lock is coordination only. :::warn The lease clock is not the worker's authority A worker must not decide that an expired local timer gives it permission to continue. The coordinator and the protected resource define ownership; the worker only holds a revocable claim. ::: :::deep Redlock and other lock algorithms still need an explicit failure model. Ask what happens during clock skew, process pause, coordinator failover and network partition instead of treating a successful client call as a proof of mutual exclusion. The existing fintech note reaches the same conclusion: a lock may reduce contention, but the database must arbitrate money correctness (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q6). :::

sections.title: Choose the authority before the mechanism

items.q: When should a database constraint or transaction beat a distributed lock?
items.a:
When the invariant already lives in one database, serialize and validate it there before adding another coordinator. A database can combine the read, decision and write with the same transaction and recovery model that owns the data. 
UPDATE inventory
SET remaining = remaining - 1
WHERE sku = :sku
  AND remaining > 0;
-- affected rows = 1: this transaction won
-- affected rows = 0: sold out or another writer won
Other strong choices include a unique constraint for one logical operation, an optimistic version predicate, or a row lock inside a short transaction. A Redis lock around the same database write may lower contention, but it cannot replace the constraint: failover, expiry or a bypassing client can still reach the database.
InvariantPreferWhy
One order id onceUnique key + idempotent resultThe database rejects duplicates
Stock never below zeroConditional decrementThe predicate and write are one decision
One row's state transitionTransaction + version/row lockRecovery follows the data
External non-transactional deviceLock + fencing + device-side rejectThe device must reject stale owners
:::tip Boundary test If a second client can write the authoritative store without consulting the lock, the lock cannot be the only correctness mechanism. Put the invariant where every writer must pass. ::: :::deep A misplaced lock often signals a misplaced service boundary. If two pieces of money or inventory must change atomically, keeping them behind one local ACID boundary is usually cheaper and safer than coordinating two services (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q5). :::

items.q: What do FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED mean, and when is each safe?
items.a:
These are database concurrency choices, not interchangeable lock flavours.
ClauseBehaviourUse it for
FOR UPDATEWait for and hold write-intent row locks until commit or rollback.A short transaction that must inspect then update the same rows.
NOWAITReturn an error immediately if a requested row is locked.Fail-fast UI/API paths with an explicit retry or conflict response.
SKIP LOCKEDSkip rows currently locked by another transaction.Queue-like work where any eligible job is acceptable.
A worker claim can look like this: 
BEGIN;
SELECT id
FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'READY'
ORDER BY id
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
LIMIT 1;
UPDATE jobs
SET status = 'RUNNING', claimed_by = :worker
WHERE id = :id;
COMMIT;
SKIP LOCKED deliberately returns an inconsistent view. It is useful for a queue, but not for a report, balance calculation or general transaction that needs a complete snapshot. The database still owns the claim; the worker needs a timeout, retry and recovery state. :::warn Do not use SKIP LOCKED to hide contention Skipping a locked row is a scheduling policy, not a correctness proof. If every row is skipped, expose backlog and retry rather than silently reporting that no work exists. ::: :::deep Locking semantics depend on the engine, index and isolation level. For example, InnoDB range scans can take gap/next-key locks, while a unique indexed lookup may lock a narrower record. Measure the actual query plan and lock graph; never infer the footprint from the SQL keyword alone (05-db-core-index-lock.transactions-mvcc-locking.q1). :::

items.q: How should PostgreSQL advisory locks be used without creating invisible ownership?
items.a:
PostgreSQL advisory locks are application-defined locks. They are useful when the key is not a row in a table, but PostgreSQL does not enforce that every code path respects the same key. The application owns the meaning. Choose the lifetime deliberately: - Transaction-level advisory locks release automatically at commit or rollback and fit short critical sections. - Session-level advisory locks survive a transaction rollback and remain until explicit unlock or session termination. They can be useful for a long-lived role, but a leaked session can retain them. - Inspect held locks through pg_locks; remember the server has a finite lock memory budget. 
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtextextended(:resource, 0));
-- read, validate and write the protected database state
COMMIT; -- the transaction-level lock is released here
Use a stable, namespaced key derivation and document the owner. Never mix a session-level acquire with a transaction-level release by accident, and do not assume an advisory lock protects a resource that another service can change directly. :::tip Database lock, database authority Advisory locks are attractive when the database is already the authority. They are not a general replacement for a unique constraint or conditional update, and they do not coordinate a remote API that cannot see PostgreSQL. ::: :::deep The official PostgreSQL model distinguishes session and transaction lifetimes and exposes both through pg_locks. That detail matters during connection-pool reuse: a session-level lock belongs to the physical session, not to the request that happened to borrow it. :::

items.q: What is the safe single-instance Redis lock pattern, and what does it still not solve?
items.a:
For a short coordination lease, generate a unique owner token, acquire atomically with one SET, and release with an atomic compare-and-delete. Never release by blindly deleting the key: a new owner may have acquired it after the old TTL expired. 
SET lock:invoice:42 owner-token NX PX 30000
-- release only if this client still owns the key
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
end
return 0
The unique token prevents an old client from deleting a newer owner's lock. The TTL gives liveness after a crash. Neither proves that the old client stopped before expiry, and a replication/failover design may have its own acknowledged-write and lock-state semantics. A critical external write needs fencing or an authoritative transactional store.
ControlWhy it existsWhat it does not guarantee
Unique tokenRelease only your own acquisitionThat you still own it after TTL
NXOne successful acquire at the keyFairness or durable business state
PXRecovery from a dead holderStale-work prevention
Compare-and-deleteSafe release under racesAtomicity with another database/API
:::warn Redis is not a magic correctness layer Use this pattern for coordination where occasional duplicate work is harmless or the resource enforces a stronger guard. For money, inventory and irreversible side effects, keep the database/idempotency/fencing check on the correctness path. ::: :::deep The Redis documentation describes this as a canonical starting point and also documents Redlock as a multi-instance algorithm. Choosing the multi-instance algorithm does not remove the need to state the failure model, bound the work, monitor renewal and protect the downstream resource from stale owners. :::

items.q: When do etcd, ZooKeeper or Kubernetes Lease fit better than a cache lock?
items.a:
Use a coordination system with an explicit session, lease and quorum model when the job is leadership or cluster coordination rather than cache admission.
SystemStrong fitDesign question
etcdLease-backed mutex and leader election in a quorum-backed control plane.What happens when the client session or keepalive is lost?
ZooKeeperEphemeral/sequential coordination recipes and ordered waiters.Can clients watch only their predecessor instead of waking a herd?
Kubernetes LeaseController leader election and heartbeats through the Kubernetes API.Is the Lease name scoped and collision-free for every deployment?
RedisShort, low-latency coordination close to an existing cache.Is the weaker failure/failover contract acceptable?
The authority must match the decision. A Kubernetes Lease can select one controller, but it does not automatically fence writes to a database. An etcd election can select a leader, but the leader still needs idempotent reconciliation after restart. :::tip Do not choose by brand Write down quorum, session loss, failover, watch/retry semantics, fencing, latency and operational ownership. A more sophisticated coordinator is not automatically safer if the protected resource ignores its ownership signal. ::: :::deep Kubernetes recommends product/component-specific Lease names to avoid collisions. etcd elections bind leadership to a lease, so expiry or revocation transfers leadership. These are useful operational contracts, but the controller should still stop issuing work after losing its session and should reconcile state on the next leadership term. :::

sections.title: Design for expiry and stale work

items.q: What must a lock acquire, release and renewal contract specify?
items.a:
A lock API is incomplete when it only says acquire(key). Make ownership and failure visible in the contract.
PartMinimum contract
KeyCanonical, namespaced resource identity; no accidental tenant collision.
OwnerUnique acquisition token; never identify ownership only by hostname or thread.
WaitBounded wait and an explicit busy result; no infinite retry hidden in a request thread.
ReleaseCompare owner before deleting or resigning; release is safe to retry.
RenewalServer/session keepalive, deadline and behaviour when renewal fails.
LossStop, fence, or transition to UNKNOWN; never continue silently.
The caller should know whether it acquired the lock, timed out, lost the lease, or completed the protected action. Do not flatten all four outcomes into a generic exception and let a retry run the action again. :::tip Make ownership a value Carry owner_token, lease_id and, when needed, fencing_token through logs, database writes and downstream calls. A lock that cannot be correlated is hard to debug and harder to prove safe. ::: :::deep In a pooled application, the owner is the logical execution, not merely the Redis connection or database session. On retry, create a new acquisition token; never reuse a token from an attempt whose outcome is unknown. :::

items.q: How should TTL, renewal and critical-section length be chosen?
items.a:
Start with a bounded work model, not a round number copied from a blog. A lease must cover the maximum expected critical work plus process pauses, network delay, coordinator failover and a renewal margin. A p99 duration is useful for capacity, but it is not a safety proof for the worst pause. 
critical work p99       = 2.0s
worst measured pause    = 1.5s
network/failover margin = 1.0s
renewal margin          = 1.5s
initial TTL             = at least 6.0s, then validate with failure tests
Renew before the deadline, preferably through the coordinator's session/keepalive mechanism. If renewal fails, stop starting new side effects, mark the attempt lost, and let the resource-side guard decide whether an in-flight write is accepted. If the work cannot be bounded, checkpoint it into restartable chunks instead of stretching a lease indefinitely. :::warn Renewal is not ownership forever A successful renewal extends a lease only while the coordinator accepts it. Treat a timeout, lost session or failed heartbeat as ownership loss; do not keep renewing from a process that no longer has a valid session. ::: :::deep Monitor the distribution of hold time and renewal latency, not just the configured TTL. Alert when p99 hold time approaches the renewal budget, when renewals fail, or when expired owners still emit writes. Those signals reveal a protocol that is already unsafe before a duplicate becomes a customer incident. :::

items.q: How do fencing tokens stop a stale lease holder from writing?
items.a:
A fencing token is a monotonically increasing number issued with each successful ownership term. The protected resource stores the greatest token it has accepted and rejects a write carrying an older token. 
-- resource-side check: the storage enforces the ordering
UPDATE device_command
SET payload = :payload,
    last_fence = :token
WHERE device_id = :device
  AND :token > last_fence;
-- affected rows = 1: accepted
-- affected rows = 0: stale owner or unknown device
The lock service issuing token 42 does not make the device safe by itself. The database, object store, device gateway or other side-effect owner must compare the token on every write. Otherwise a paused worker can resume after token 43 and still mutate state.
LayerResponsibility
CoordinatorSerialise terms and issue increasing tokens.
WorkerAttach the current token to every protected operation.
ResourceReject a token lower than the one already accepted.
RecoveryReconcile rejected or unknown operations idempotently.
:::tip The token must reach the authority A fencing token in a log line is not fencing. It becomes a safety mechanism only when the final writer checks it atomically with the state change. ::: :::deep For resources that cannot store a token, use their own version/ETag/sequence precondition if available. If there is no conditional write at all, describe the lock as best-effort coordination and do not promise strict mutual exclusion to the business. :::

items.q: What should a worker do after it loses the lock in the middle of work?
items.a:
Stop treating the result as success. The worker should stop new writes, record the ownership-loss reason, and move the operation to a state that can be reconciled. Whether already-sent work happened is often UNKNOWN, not FAILED.

A robust workflow separates the coordination attempt from the business state:

1. Create or load an idempotency record.
2. Acquire a lease and record the owner term/token.
3. Perform a bounded, idempotent step with the token.
4. On renewal failure, stop and mark the attempt UNKNOWN or RETRYABLE.
5. Query the resource or consume its callback before deciding the next transition.
6. Reconcile later; never run a blind compensating action just because the lock was lost.

A lock loss is not a reason to refund, decrement again, or publish a second event. Idempotency keys, conditional state transitions and reconciliation close the gap (09-distributed-tx-fintech.correctness-where-money-is-involved.q1).

:::warn Do not convert timeout into failure
A network timeout says the caller lacks evidence. It does not say the remote side did nothing. Keep PENDING/UNKNOWN visible until a status query, callback or reconciliation source proves the outcome.
:::

:::deep
For batch work, checkpoint after each durable unit and make the unit safe to repeat.

For external APIs, reuse the provider idempotency key.

For database work, let a transaction commit or roll back locally and let an outbox publish the next step; do not hold a distributed lock across a slow remote call unless the failure contract justifies it.
:::

items.q: Which pattern should a scheduler, resource worker or controller use?
items.a:
Choose the pattern from the unit of work and the authority that can observe completion.
NeedPreferred shapeWhy
One active scheduler/controllerLeader election + lease + idempotent reconciliationStandby replicas can take over the role.
One operation per resource keyShort lock or database serialization + fencing when neededOnly conflicting keys block each other.
Many independent jobsDurable queue or database claim with retry stateWork is visible, retryable and recoverable.
One invariant in one databaseLocal transaction, constraint or conditional writeThe authority decides correctness directly.
A global lock around a queue often creates a bottleneck and hides backlog. A leader election around per-order work makes one replica unnecessarily responsible for everything. Keep the coordination scope as small as the conflict scope. :::tip Name the conflict set Say exactly which two operations cannot overlap: inventory:sku-42, scheduler:settlement, or tenant:17:rebuild. If the key is just global, the design probably has not found its real invariant. ::: :::deep The same decision applies to Spring jobs: multiple replicas need election or a lock to avoid duplicate scheduling, but the job itself should be restartable and idempotent. A lease is not a substitute for a durable work state (25-microservice.08-operational-concerns.q2). :::

items.q: Why do idempotency and outbox still matter when a distributed lock is present?
items.a:
A lock serializes overlapping attempts; it does not remember whether a previous attempt completed, and it does not make a retry after timeout safe. A process can lose its lease after committing the business change but before publishing an event or returning a response. Use a durable idempotency record for the logical operation, and write the record/business change/outbox event in one local transaction where possible: 
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO idempotency(key, status)
VALUES (:key, 'IN_PROGRESS');
-- unique conflict means another attempt owns this logical operation
UPDATE order_state SET status = 'PAID' WHERE order_id = :id;
INSERT INTO outbox(event_key, payload) VALUES (:key, :event);
COMMIT;
-- publisher retries the outbox; consumer deduplicates event_key
The lock may reduce duplicate pressure, but the unique key and state transition remain the guard. This is why a lock belongs around coordination while outbox/idempotency belong around durable meaning (09-distributed-tx-fintech.distributed-transaction-patterns.q3). :::warn Never make the lock your only deduplication record If the lock key expires, is evicted, or is deleted during failover, a second attempt must still be rejected or made harmless by the authoritative state. ::: :::deep Keep the lock out of a long remote transaction when possible: reserve local state, commit, publish via outbox, and let the consumer perform an idempotent transition. If a remote call returns UNKNOWN, reconcile by idempotency key rather than acquiring a new lock and sending a new command. :::

items.q: Which metrics and logs reveal a distributed-lock problem before users do?
items.a:
Instrument the protocol as a queue with ownership, not just as a boolean success flag. - **Acquire:** attempts, successes, busy/timeouts, wait duration and retry count by resource class. - **Hold:** critical-section duration, p50/p95/p99, maximum hold and key cardinality. - **Lease:** renew success/failure, remaining TTL at renewal, session loss and expired leases. - **Safety:** fencing-token rejects, stale-owner writes, duplicate state transitions and UNKNOWN outcomes. - **Operations:** owner churn, hot keys, dead-letter/reconciliation backlog and recovery time after coordinator loss. Log a correlation id, resource key, owner token hash, lease id and fencing token where safe; never log credentials or the full token if it is a bearer secret. Keep metrics low-cardinality by grouping keys into resource classes rather than putting an unbounded user id in a label.
SignalInterpretationFirst action
Wait p99 risingContention or work duration is growing.Find hot keys and shorten/partition the critical section.
Renew failuresPause, network or coordinator health is degrading.Stop new side effects and inspect session loss.
Fencing rejectsStale work reached the resource.Preserve evidence; fix the caller, not just the TTL.
Expired work with no retryLiveness recovered but business progress did not.Run reconciliation and expose backlog.
:::tip Alert on absence and rejection A lock can fail silently by never being renewed or by skipping every job. Alert on missing completion, fencing rejects and reconciliation age, not only on exceptions thrown by the lock client. ::: :::deep Correlate lock metrics with GC pauses, CPU throttling, database lock waits, network errors and deploys. The lock is often the first place a hidden saturation problem becomes visible, not the root cause. :::

items.q: How do you test a distributed lock so the test proves more than two clients can take turns?
items.a:
Test the failure protocol, not only the happy-path mutual exclusion. - Start two contenders for the same key and many contenders for different keys; verify conflicting work serializes while unrelated work proceeds. - Kill the holder before release; verify recovery after the lease/session deadline and no permanent lock. - Pause or stop renewals while the holder keeps running; verify the stale holder is fenced or its side effect is rejected. - Delay the network between acquire, renew and release; verify bounded outcomes and safe retry. - Crash after the business commit but before the outbox publish; verify idempotent replay and reconciliation. - Force coordinator failover, clock skew in test doubles, hot-key contention and a long database transaction; observe the documented contract. 
assert acquire(A, key) == GRANTED
pause(A) beyond lease
assert acquire(B, key) == GRANTED
assert write(resource, tokenA) == REJECTED
assert write(resource, tokenB) == ACCEPTED
assert retry(A) does not create a second business result
:::tip A useful review checklist Before approving a lock, ask: What is the authority? What happens after expiry? Who checks the fencing token? What is the bounded wait? Which state records UNKNOWN? What metric catches a stale write? How does the system recover after coordinator loss? ::: :::deep Run these tests against the real coordination and database implementations where possible. An in-memory fake can prove caller branches, but it cannot prove Redis failover, PostgreSQL lock lifetime, etcd session loss or Kubernetes API behavior. Inject faults at the boundary that owns the guarantee. :::
